chapter: Oliver's circle and old New Orleans players
title: Lee Collins and the 1946 record date he missed
summary: He could not get Lee Collins to read, left him off his 1946 session, regrets it, and recounts Lee's later years.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Remembering King Oliver: the man, the band, the decline

blocks.x: I understand Lee Collins couldn't read too well.

Who that? No, he couldn't. I tried my best to teach Lee how to read, but he just barely spelled. And it's one thing that I'll never forget concerning Lee. See Lee and I were schoolmates too. And I had this, when I recorded in 1946, we still, still do. We'll get as many New Orleans musicians as possible. I mean until today. I just recorded a few days ago and we had Brother Montgomery, Oliver, Oliver Alcorn, myself, at least there was three of us at New Orleans. You still do it today, you know. And so Lee used to play with the mouthpiece right across his bottom lip. So I kept laughing and finally I got into the corner of the trumpet like it should be. But I never could get him to do much reading, see, he was very slow. In fact he played on Clark Street, sometime he and the piano, maybe at the most three pieces. But this particular time I had a contract, I thought it was called Melrose, signed me up for the record for Victor. So I invited Lee up to the rehearsal and I had some music arranged. And it was something like, it just was some figures, you know, behind what they call riffs, behind the soloists. So after about an hour's time, Lee still couldn't play. So my time was getting shot. I regret this because I figured that there was another fellow by the name of Lewis Ogletree, who was right down there, this was at the Union. And I got him and said, I just couldn't, I didn't use Lee. And so he and I, it was a bad feeling from then on, you understand. I wasn't so with Lee, but there's some things that I figured he did. There was a fellow around, a young fellow that came to some nice money, and he was booking these bands concerts, you know. And I had rehearsed the band pretty good, and I never did get a chance to play. And I figured maybe something might happen, I don't know. But he and Lee was like this, you understand. So, but as you grow older you learn, I could have used Lee just to play some hot choruses, you see. Then I never would have lost his friendship. But you learn, you see that afterwards, you know what I'm talking about. And so, as you know, when Lee went over to Ory, he and Zuby Singleton, Melrose, not Melrose, Meshro, they went over to Europe. And Lee, something happened to his chest or throat. He came back sick, and he never did recover. He laid on about three or four years before he died. And so, I think of that sometimes, you know. He was a fellow, you know, old. It could have been another way. It could have been another way. I might have talked to the guy and said, Well, I want to use another trumpet, which would have made it three brass. But then the time, then I had trouble clearing this, Don L. Howard, he didn't show up. So I had to go and make the record without him too, so I made another enemy. He said he had to go to court. His wife was divorcing, but he didn't call me, you know, and tell me. So I used Buck Douglas the tenor. That was in the 46th when I was. You see, when you have a contract for a certain day, a certain amount of men, well, you don't want to go to the fellow and say, Well, I can't make it today, and after bed, make it next week or something like that. It just, it puts you in a bad light, I imagine, you understand? But I hated that because Lee and I attended school together. We only lived at Louisiana and me and Ferrette and I lived on the other shades between Howard and Ferrette. It's right around the county. So Lee died. And I hated that because now I see it could have been another way. Maybe I could have used him just the same, just in spots. But we did have things arranged. He would have to test it and I don't play. You know, and maybe we'd have a course and I'd give him a course or something like that. It was possible.
I understand they tried to put him in the rest of the spare for a while. Yeah.

No, he could play, he really could play. But he didn't read so well. Now a guy, Kelly, a guy Kelly could read and play good too. See, we recorded with Jimmy, you know, you ever had the records with Jimmy and the Blues, the Blues jumped the rabbit and things like that. It was different altogether. He played with South Stan. The guy was always in Baton Rouge.
